$comment: The kit's own canaries. A template that ships broken replicates across every project that copies it, so these run in CI on this repo.

canaries.guards: The backlog validator rejects a symptom too short to act on. Without this an entry can say 'broken' and still count as a tracked bug.
A dated deferral fails the build once it passes. Without this, 'revisit before the next release' becomes permanent by accident.
A neutral Bugbot conclusion carrying a completed-review summary is findings, not a skipped review. This is the exact defect that left five findings unread across three pull requests.
A GitHub API failure resolves to undetermined, never to a pass. Collapsing errors to a benign state is how a detector reports green during an outage.
canaries.find: return { state: 'undetermined', pr, detail: `could not read #${pr}: ${detail.error}` }

canaries.guards: A gap or duplicate in a rule sequence fails the build. Nine branches merging at once once produced 21-24 missing and two rules both numbered 25, with registry entries citing rules that had moved.
A source glob matching nothing fails rather than certifying that every citation resolves. Every assertion in that check is vacuously true of an empty file list.
A staleness check that cannot reach the canonical manifest fails. Passing there would report 'current' during an outage — the silent-green shape the whole kit exists to find.
A kit file edited in a consuming project fails. Otherwise it is a fix fifteen projects will not get, and a divergence the next refresh silently overwrites.
A reusable pr-check workflow that does not run the verification gate fails. Otherwise the project that adopts it gets a green check over nothing checked.
A step in the verification gate without `if: !cancelled()` fails. GitHub defaults a step to success(), so an unrelated earlier failure switches the assertion off at exactly the moment it matters.
canaries.find:
- name: No generated files tracked in git
      if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
canaries.replace: - name: No generated files tracked in git

canaries.guards: A Bugbot verdict job that gives up waiting must fail. 'Did not finish in time' is not 'found nothing', and reporting it as a pass reproduces the exact defect the job was written to fix.
canaries.find:
"Comment 'bugbot run' on the PR, or re-run this job once it has finished."
              exit 1
canaries.replace:
"Comment 'bugbot run' on the PR, or re-run this job once it has finished."
              exit 0

canaries.guards: A registry entry that has not been re-verified inside the window fails. Deferral is fine; undated deferral becomes permanent by accident, and a table of intentions keeps reading as authoritative.

A repository lookup that failed for a reason other than 404 is reported, not treated as evidence either way. Collapsing it to 'absent' cries wolf during an outage; collapsing it to 'present' certifies a tier nobody checked.
The readable fleet table cannot disagree with the checked one. A generated file nobody regenerates is a hand-maintained list wearing a disguise.
A non-GitHub remote returns null rather than a plausible-looking slug that would send API calls somewhere they cannot succeed.

A repository the credentials cannot open must not fall through to the absent branch. GitHub answers 404 both for a private repository the caller may not see and for a path that is genuinely missing, and conflating the two made the first online run of this check accuse a fully-adopted project of holding none of the kit. Rule V39.

The offline run verifies no claim against any repository, so it carries the deadline for the run that does. Removing the expiry leaves a check that cannot fail on adoption as the only one running, which is how a table of intentions keeps reading as authoritative.

Nine production sites are watched by one reusable workflow, whose Playwright step used to exit 0 when the spec file was absent. Renaming a spec silently ended live monitoring and printed a tick. Asking for the smoke and not having it must fail; not wanting it is run-playwright: false, which a reader can see in the caller.
canaries.find:
echo "::error::run-playwright is true but $spec does not exist." \
                 "Point smoke-spec at the real file, or set run-playwright: false" \
                 "and accept that nothing is watching this site's behaviour."
            exit 1

canaries.guards: A status code says a server answered, not that it served the site. The body size floor and the expected-text match are what separate a live site from a parking page, a CDN error page, or an empty 200 from a broken deploy.

An input a project can set that the gate never receives. The configuration reads as applied and does nothing, which is worse than not offering it. source-dirs was added to the assertion and not to the generator that writes these workflows, so the script the test recommends produced a workflow that failed the test.

V46. The naive main-module idiom compares a resolved file URL to a raw argv path. Through a symlinked directory they differ, the CLI never runs, and the process exits 0 — a checker reporting success having checked nothing. It was in two of this kit binaries, including the one CI uses to verify the manifest.

V48's checker giving a verdict without a denominator. Its first version printed a green tick having measured six jobs in a repository that declares forty, reporting 'all under 75% of their timeout' while examining none of the ones anyone worried about.

V50. The jobs endpoint pages at 30 and reports the truth only in total_count. Reading page one and calling it the run drops exactly the jobs this check exists to watch, since matrix legs are what push a run past thirty — and coverage still counts the declaration as seen from page one, so the verdict is green over a truncated sample.

The drift checker warns and exits 0 one release behind, rather than failing. Without this the commonest situation is a red build, the fleet reads the red as noise, and a locally modified kit hides inside it.
The tolerance for being behind expires on a date. Without this an undated leniency becomes permanent by accident and the fail-above-one-minor half never fires.

check-backlog --verify-prs fails when an entry and its pull request disagree. Without this the plan of record can claim in-review against a merged PR indefinitely, which six entries across the fleet did.
assert-tests-executed names each test that only passed on a retry. Without this the run prints a count, exits 0, and the failing test is findable only by reading the JSON report by hand.

A citation is a number on the same line as the word rule. Without this a sentence ending in 'rules' above a line starting with a digit is reported as a dangling citation, and the repair is to weaken the checker.
The manifest writer takes an explicit release version. Without it the bump counts runs, and two runs in one change put every consumer more than one minor behind, which now fails rather than warns.

The tier-2 wiring check pairs a report and a floor within one mapping. Without the scoping it takes the first of each from the joined workflows, so an earlier empty report hides a real pair and a report in one job certifies a floor in another.
canaries.find: const sameBlock = (line, indent) => line.trim() === '' || indentOf(line) >= indent

canaries.guards: A test.fail() case — one asserting something is broken — is not reported as an intermittent failure. Counting any failed attempt as a retry made this check invent flakiness, and a repository with a budget of 0 would go red over tests behaving exactly as written.
A test that timed out and passed on the retry is named. The commonest intermittent shape there is, and the first version of the detector looked only for the literal status failed.

A rulebook section number such as comprehensive rules 1-2-1-1-1 is not read as citing local rule 1-2. A citation may no more be followed by -<digit> than by .<digit>, both being section numbers rather than rules. Anchored on that lookahead pair rather than on the whole pattern, because an anchor spanning the entire regex is invalidated by every narrowing — twice so far.

An impossible answer — a consumer ahead of canonical — is confirmed against an uncached read before it fails the build. Two repositories went red three minutes after a release because the CDN had not caught up, and a check that reddens for a reason unrelated to what it guards teaches that the check is noise.

The entry describing the pull request under review is exempt when written as landed, and refused when written as in-review. Without this there is no honest status for that entry: in-review is false the moment it merges and landed is false while it is open, so the default branch goes red after every merge and the gate stops being one.

A local prefix may contain a letter without beginning with one. 4thcltr.com uses 4C, so requiring a leading letter skipped its citations entirely — reporting that every citation resolves, which is the worse of the two directions a coverage matcher can fail in.

A number beginning with zero is not a citation, because no sequence starts at zero. towit.io vendors two copies of AngularJS whose pluralization comment says "three explicit number rules 0, 1 and 2", and the check is not wired there — so it was a false failure waiting for whoever wired it first.

The monitor's curl format ends with a newline. Without it `read` reports failure at EOF though it has assigned every variable, and under set -e the step dies before printing the URL it was checking — which took live monitoring for all nine sites down between 2026-09-07 and 2026-09-11 while looking like an infrastructure hiccup (V61).

Playwright's install runs under the same condition as the smoke that needs it. Mismatched, an earlier failure skips the install while the smoke proceeds, and the run's error becomes a missing npm package rather than the fault that occurred.
canaries.find:
- name: Setup Node for Playwright
        if: ${{ !cancelled() && inputs.run-playwright }}
canaries.replace:
- name: Setup Node for Playwright
        if: inputs.run-playwright

canaries.guards: The shared deploy writes into the existing inode. Without --inplace rsync renames a temp file over the target, and over the CIFS mount that serves these sites the container keeps a handle to the deleted inode: every request for that path then returns 500 until the container is restarted. It does not expire, and a reload does not clear it (V61).

A failed rsync is the function's answer, whatever the steps after it would report. A caller writing `nas_ssh_rsync_to … || handle` disables errexit inside the function, so without an explicit status the live check's 200 became the verdict on a deploy that transferred nothing — found by pointing anal0g's prune at a source path that does not exist and watching it exit 0.
canaries.find:
if [[ "${status}" -ne 0 ]]; then
    echo "rsync exited ${status}. Not repairing permissions and not checking the" \
      "site, because neither would describe this deploy." >&2
    return "${status}"
  fi

canaries.guards: The post-deploy live check accepts a 200 or a redirect and nothing else. Widened to any answer at all, a 500 from the site reads as a successful deploy — which is how eleven sites came to be deployed with nothing asking whether they still served.
Deploying a fleet domain fetches the site by itself. A verification each repository has to opt into is one that some repository will not have, and this fleet has ten deploy scripts.
A site that does not serve fails the deploy. Returning success from the check leaves the operator's last line reading "Deploy complete", which is the precise shape of the outage this rule came from.

The live URL is read from fleet.json rather than guessed from the directory name, so a staging target like bindercurve.com-dev is not probed at a hostname nobody serves and then reported as a broken deploy.

A bare `rule 12` cites the shared document whether or not the project also keeps local rules. When it addressed whichever list the project numbered its own rules in, adopting a local prefix silently rewrote every citation already in the repository: bindercurve.com added two local rules and 34 citations across six files stopped resolving in one commit.
canaries.find:
const cited = Number(raw)
    if (cited < 1 || cited > sharedNumbers.length) {
